extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and policymakers in political science, media economics, journalism studies, and communications research
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for analyzing how media market structure, ownership, technology, and regulation shape news content and its political effects, and for measuring changes in that content. Emphasizes empirical methods and dimensions for cross-sectional and historical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda setting, framing, and priming
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominent media effects analyzed in political science include agenda setting (media defining which issues are important), framing (how the description of a choice/event affects reaction), and priming (media helping define the events/issues used to judge politicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are core dimensions for evaluating media influence. Tracing whether and how these effects influence voting is difficult. Use laboratory experiments, internet experiments, and careful survey analysis (especially reinterview/panel data) to isolate effects. See cited empirical and experimental literature (e.g., Druckman for framing; Miller and Krosnick for priming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenges in measuring media effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Key empirical obstacles: verifying that a person received a particular media message; determining the exact content consumed; knowing baseline opinions before exposure; and separating media influence from other causes when media respond to events and politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address with lab/Internet experiments (control exposure), panel/reinterview surveys (observe changes), careful measurement models, and attention to measurement error (which can bias effect sizes). Explicitly document exposure, attention, comprehension, and recall when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard/soft news mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an outlet/program devotes coverage to 'hard' public affairs (e.g., legislative votes, Supreme Court cases, policymaking data) versus 'soft' news (human interest, celebrity, entertainment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify by counting stories or time devoted to policymaking-relevant items (e.g., Congressional Quarterly votes, Harvard Law Review cases) versus soft subjects (e.g., People magazine features). Use content coding of story topics and time/space measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political orientation of the news outlet
rubrics_metrics.description: The left–right world view or ideological slant an outlet conveys in coverage and selection of stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure orientation via content coding (tone, source selection, story placement), audience perception, and comparison of issue emphasis across outlets. Consider how orientation interacts with audience targeting and advertiser markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language use and style of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences across outlets in language, rhetorical devices, narrative style, and presentation conventions that affect how information is perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify stylistic dimensions (tone, emotional language, use of anecdotes vs data), analyze framing devices, and code for readability and rhetorical strategies. Style can signal soft vs hard orientation and affect public reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on news personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an outlet's brand and content rely on personalities (anchors, commentators) rather than institutionally-driven reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess airtime/column space given to named personalities, branded segments, and opinion-driven formats. High personality dependence can shift content toward opinion and entertainment and affect advertiser/brand positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership structure (state/public vs commercial)
rubrics_metrics.description: How ownership (state-controlled, public broadcaster, commercial conglomerate, or locally owned) shapes objectives, incentives, and types of coverage offered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the outlet is motivated by public-service objectives (education, national identity, positive externalities) or profit (advertiser valuation). Public/state outlets may invest in expensive international/investigative reporting or propagate propaganda; commercial outlets target consumers and advertisers, favoring content that attracts valuable demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit motivations and cost constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which outlets factor production costs and advertiser returns into decisions about which stories to cover and how much to invest in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure resource allocation to investigative/international coverage vs cheaper soft-news ingredients. Document changes in staffing, use of wire/video services, and outsourcing which can reduce depth/quality. Consider how cost reductions can decrease depth while increasing breadth of options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel proliferation and competition (spatial model)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the number of channels/entrants and their strategic product-location decisions (low/medium/high public affairs content) affect the distribution of programming across the news spectrum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spatial/product-location models to predict shifts: initial entrants may cluster in moderate/soft niches; increased channels raise fragmentation and can increase soft-news offerings. Evaluate equilibrium placement, incentives to switch genres, and how public broadcasters' presence affects commercial entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting and market segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets differentiate by targeting demographic or partisan segments (e.g., tabloids vs business papers; urban vs rural; black-targeted media), affecting story choice and slant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure audience composition, advertiser valuation of demographics, and the mix of topics tailored to target groups. Track how outlets tailor content (e.g., human interest, sports) to attract advertiser-valued viewers and the political implications (e.g., turnout effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth versus breadth tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition can increase the number of choices (breadth) while simultaneously reducing the depth/quality of coverage (e.g., investigative reporting) in some niches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify depth (investigative hours, original reporting, analysis) and breadth (number of distinct outlets/programs covering a niche). Look for 'race to the bottom' dynamics when cost pressures and entrant incentives reduce average depth despite more offerings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herding and originality/diversity of perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency of journalists to follow established angles as more reporters cover a story, which can reduce the number of original takes and magnify early errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure incidence of story copying, source overlap, and convergence of angles across outlets. Examine penalties/organizational incentives for deviating from perceived consensus. Herding can be more pronounced under speed/attention pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication and diversity under separate ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive duplication (multiple outlets offering similar programming) can reduce overall diversity compared to monopoly ownership, depending on audience preference splits (Steiner model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare program types offered under monopoly vs separate ownership; quantify audience left unserved by competing duplication. Use models and empirical counts of unique program types to assess diversity effects from ownership structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet and digital dissemination effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect of the Internet, blogs, email, and text messaging on story circulation, speed of dissemination, and constraints on traditional media’s ability to ignore stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence and influence of blogs, social media/blog-originated stories, and rapid grassroots circulation. Account for low marginal distribution costs but persistent fixed costs (branding, advertising to attract attention). Evaluate whether digital lowers barriers for hard-news providers or reinforces incumbents due to attention limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed of transmission and its effect on analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Faster transmission (satellite, Internet) increases immediacy of coverage but may reduce time for reasoned analysis and increase herding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure turnaround times for stories, prevalence of 'breaking' coverage vs follow-up in-depth analysis, and correlations between speed and analytical depth. Examine organizational incentives for rapid publication and how they interact with audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property rights, legal, and regulatory constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: How defamation laws, licensing requirements, censorship, Internet filtering, and campaign finance/election laws shape editorial choices and topic avoidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the legal/regulatory environment and evidence of self-censorship (avoidance of controversial topics), licensing conditions (local partners), and penalties that alter risk calculations for investigative reporting. Consider shadow of future state action in assessing content choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to measuring changes in media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Three outlined empirical approaches: (1) product differentiation analysis, (2) information search patterns, and (3) consumption/production surveys, typically using cross-sectional snapshots or historical samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement content sampling (past vs present), quantify multiple product dimensions (hard/soft mix, political orientation, language, style, personality dependence), and combine with audience/production surveys to infer motivations and effects. Use reinterview/panel data where possible to measure impact over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of exposure and reception (who 'gets the news')
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating who is exposed to news, pays attention, comprehends, and remembers it is crucial to infer media effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect measures of exposure, attention, comprehension, and recall in surveys or experiments. Use general prior knowledge measures as proxies for reception when direct exposure metrics are weak (Price and Zaller). Adjust for differential reception across segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of policymaking-relevant content
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which outlets incorporate data and events directly used in policymaking processes (key legislative votes, major court cases, indices used by interest groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track coverage of those defined items (e.g., Congressional Quarterly votes, Harvard Law Review cases) as an indicator of serving a 'producer demand' for political information. Compare presence across outlets and over time to assess civic informational provision.
